# ChoiceBoard

ChoiceBoard is group decision-making software. Teams define options and factors, answer quick head-to-head comparisons, and get a ranked result with a measured level of agreement — a decision they can defend.

Source: https://choiceboard.io/

Group decision-making software 

# Stop debating. Start deciding.

ChoiceBoard is group decision-making software. Teams define options and factors, answer quick head-to-head comparisons, and get a ranked result with a measured level of agreement — a decision they can defend.

[Start free →](https://choiceboard.io/#pricing) [See how it works](https://choiceboard.io/#how-it-works)

How it works 

## How to make a group decision in four steps

No training, no facilitation degree, no 40-tab spreadsheet. Frame the decision once — ChoiceBoard handles the structure, the math, and the diplomacy.

1

### Frame the decision

Name your project, list the options on the table, and add the factors that matter — or keep it simple with an overall comparison.

2

### Invite anyone

Share a private link or send email invites. Participants need zero accounts and zero onboarding — they just click and go.

3

### Compare, one pair at a time

Everyone answers simple head-to-head questions: “Which option is better for cost?” Ten seconds each, on any device.

4

### Get a defensible answer

A statistically ranked result with confidence, agreement, and what drove the outcome — ready to present, share, or export.

Why teams switch 

## Your decision matrix, minus the spreadsheet fights

A weighted decision matrix sounds rigorous — until five people invent scores from thin air, anchor on the loudest voice, and argue over cell C7. ChoiceBoard gets you the rigor without the theater.

### No made-up numbers

Nobody has to decide whether “flexibility” is a 7 or an 8. Simple either-or judgments do the work, and the model computes the scores.

### No anchoring, no groupthink

Everyone compares independently, so the quiet expert counts as much as the confident VP. Disagreement is surfaced, not steamrolled.

### Weights earned, not guessed

Factor importance comes from the same head-to-head process — so “what matters most” reflects your team, not one person's gut.

Built for real groups 

## Everyone weighs in. You stay in control.

Collecting input shouldn't mean handing out admin access — or chasing people for a week. Invite participants with a link, and decide exactly what each person sees.

### Frictionless participation

No accounts, no downloads. Participants open a link on any device and answer one focused question at a time — with autosave and resume.

### Tiered result access

Compare only, compare and see your own results, or full report access. You choose per invite — and every link is revocable.

### Live participation tracking

See who's opened, who's mid-way, and who's done. Nudge the stragglers, close input on your deadline, and lock the result.

The moment of truth 

## Results you can defend in any boardroom

“Trust me” isn't a methodology. ChoiceBoard's Bayesian ranking engine shows the answer *and* the evidence — so your decision survives the toughest question in the room: “How did you get this?”

### A clear recommendation

Pick-one projects surface a recommended option with its lead over the runner-up. Rank-all projects deliver a full priority order with natural tiers.

### Confidence & agreement, quantified

See how solid the ranking is, how aligned the group is, and exactly where people disagree — before you commit, not after.

### What actually moved the needle

Factor importance, differentiation, and decision leverage show which trade-offs drove the outcome — and which were noise.

### Ready to present

Preliminary vs. final states, print and export views, and controlled sharing — walk into the meeting with the answer, not another meeting.

Informed meetings 

## Walk in aligned. Talk about what actually matters.

Most decision meetings are people trading opinions from memory. With ChoiceBoard, everyone arrives looking at the same collective ranking and factor weights — so the conversation is about real substance, not idiosyncratic takes, and its essence is captured.

### One shared view of the group's thinking

Collective rankings and factor weights on one screen — everyone sees the same evidence, so nobody's arguing from a different set of facts.

### Spend the meeting on the real disagreements

ChoiceBoard shows exactly where the group splits — so you skip the parts everyone already agrees on and dig into the trade-offs that matter.

### The decision's essence, captured

What was chosen, why, how confident the group was, and who disagreed — recorded and shareable, so nobody relitigates it in six weeks.

FAQ 

## Frequently asked questions

What is group decision-making software?

It's software that gives a team a structured way to choose between options together. Instead of long meetings and biased spreadsheets, ChoiceBoard collects each person's input through simple head-to-head comparisons and combines them into a single ranked result — with confidence and agreement metrics so you know how solid the answer is.

How is ChoiceBoard different from a weighted decision matrix spreadsheet?

A weighted decision matrix combines scores for options with weights for criteria. ChoiceBoard collects head-to-head comparisons instead of asking participants for numeric scores. The result includes a ranking and a measured level of agreement. ChoiceBoard doesn’t hide disagreement, it measures it.

What is pairwise comparison?

A pairwise comparison is a judgment between two options at a time. In ChoiceBoard, participants answer head-to-head questions about options and factors. The comparisons contribute to a ranked result with a measured level of agreement.

Do participants need an account to give input?

No. You invite participants with a private share link or email invitation. They open it on any device, answer one question at a time, and are done in minutes. You control exactly what each person can see — from compare-only up to the full results report — and every link can be revoked or expired.

What kinds of decisions is ChoiceBoard good for?

Any decision with multiple options and multiple stakeholders: vendor and software selection, feature and roadmap prioritization, hiring panels, budget allocation, naming and creative reviews, and strategy trade-offs. Use Pick-one mode when you need a single winner, or Rank-all mode when you need a full priority order.

How does the free tier work?

The Starter plan is a free tier for individuals and small teams. It includes 2 active projects, up to 20 responses, Pick-one and Rank-all modes, and the core results view. Upgrade when you need more projects, more admins, unlimited participants, or the full results suite.

# Group decision making process for teams

Your team has options, opinions, and another meeting on the calendar. A group decision making process gives that conversation a structure: define the call, decide who makes it, compare the options, and record the reasoning. Start with a clear question before you collect another vote.

**The ChoiceBoard team** · 5-minute read

Published September 7, 2026 · Updated September 7, 2026

**Key takeaways**

- Atlassian’s decision framework assigns one Approver to make the decision.

- Atlassian’s decision document includes evidence, factors, and options.

- Atlassian recommends recording the decision and its rationale.

- ChoiceBoard combines head-to-head input into a ranked result with a measured level of agreement.

## How do you make a decision as a group without endless meetings?

For a group decision, agree on the question, decision owner, and evaluation factors before gathering input. Use the meeting to examine unresolved trade-offs and make the call. The workflow below is our practical recommendation, not a claim about a guaranteed reduction in meeting time.

A group decision-making process is a sequence for gathering people’s input and reaching a choice. The group can contribute without every participant having the same decision authority. Make that distinction explicit at the start.

1. ### Frame the decision

  Write the decision as a question with a clear boundary. For example: “Which of these options should we choose for the next project?” Add the deadline, the constraints, and what would make an option unacceptable. This is a hypothetical prompt, not a customer example.

  Keep separate decisions separate. Choosing a supplier and agreeing on next year’s budget need different questions, even when the same people attend.
 
2. ### Assign the decision roles

  One available framework is Driver, Approver, Contributors, and Informed (DACI). In [Atlassian’s DACI play](https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/daci), the Driver organizes the work, one Approver makes the decision, Contributors provide expertise, and Informed stakeholders receive the outcome.

  If you choose a different authority model, write that down instead. Tell participants whether they are advising, voting, or jointly approving. Do this before their preferred option is known.
 
3. ### Compare the same options against the same factors

  Prepare a shared description of each option. List the factors you want people to consider, then attach the evidence available for each one. Atlassian’s decision document similarly calls for relevant data, decision factors, and a table of options.

  Ask participants to record their judgments and reasons before the discussion. Leave room for “I don’t know.” A missing answer is a prompt to gather evidence, not an invitation to invent a score.
 
4. ### Review dissent and record the call

  Bring the unresolved differences into the conversation. Ask whether people disagree about the evidence, the importance of a factor, or the acceptable trade-off. Keep those questions separate as you work through them.

  Then have the designated owner make the call. Atlassian’s follow-up guidance recommends documenting the final decision so future teams can understand how and why it was reached. Record the remaining concerns alongside the outcome.

## What should a team decision record include?

A team decision record should let someone reconstruct the choice without attending the meeting. We recommend the following fields. Copy them into the document your team already uses.

Suggested decision record

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Decision and owner | The question, who makes the call, and the date. |
| Options and constraints | What was considered and which requirements had to be met. |
| Factors and evidence | What mattered, the supporting sources, and unresolved assumptions. |
| Outcome and dissent | The choice, its rationale, and the concerns that remain. |
| Next action | Who acts next and what new evidence would justify revisiting the choice. |

## How do you get buy-in on a decision people disagree with?

For a decision people disagree with, start by showing how their input was considered. Explain the trade-off the owner accepted and name any concern that remains open. Do not ask people to describe disagreement as consensus.

Our recommendation is to separate acknowledgment from agreement. A participant can confirm that the record represents their view while still preferring another option. Give them a way to correct the record before the team acts on it.

## Where does ChoiceBoard fit in the process?

ChoiceBoard structures the comparison step. Teams define options and factors, answer head-to-head questions, and receive a ranked result with a measured level of agreement. The person who has to make the call still brings the judgment.

> ChoiceBoard doesn’t hide disagreement, it measures it.
> 
> 
> 
> The ChoiceBoard team

Choose a comparison format that fits the decision. Use the [decision matrix template](https://choiceboard.io/blog/templates/decision-matrix-template/) for explicit weighted scoring, or read the [pairwise comparison guide](https://choiceboard.io/blog/guides/pairwise-comparison-method/) for head-to-head judgments.

## Frequently asked questions

Who should make the final group decision?

Agree on decision authority before collecting input. In DACI, one Approver makes the final decision. Other processes may assign authority differently; tell participants which process you are using.

Does a group decision require everyone to agree?

That depends on the decision rule you choose. A process with a designated decision owner can collect group input without requiring unanimous approval. Record unresolved disagreement accurately.

What should you do when the team lacks evidence?

Record the gap, assign someone to investigate it, and state whether the decision can wait. We recommend keeping unknowns visible rather than filling them with unsupported scores.

What should you save after making a group decision?

Save the decision, owner, options, factors, supporting evidence, rationale, and remaining concerns. Add the next action and the conditions under which you would revisit the choice.

# Pairwise comparison method for team decisions

Your team can discuss every option and still leave the ordering unresolved. The pairwise comparison method narrows each judgment to two options at a time. Start with a focused question, collect the comparisons, and examine what those judgments do and do not establish.

**The ChoiceBoard team** · 5-minute read

Published September 7, 2026 · Updated September 7, 2026

**Key takeaways**

- A pairwise comparison evaluates two options at a time.

- Five options have 10 distinct pairs when every pair is compared once.

- Pairwise preferences can form a cycle instead of a consistent order.

- A ranking and a measured level of agreement describe different aspects of a ChoiceBoard result.

## What is a pairwise comparison and when should a team use one?

A pairwise comparison is a judgment between two alternatives. Use a head-to-head question when you want participants to express a preference between a specific pair, rather than assign separate numeric ratings. The [1000minds method guide](https://www.1000minds.com/decision-making/pairwise-comparison) explains this two-at-a-time approach.

Our recommendation is to use a clearly defined factor for each question. “Which option is better for implementation fit?” gives the participant a stated basis for comparison. “Which is best?” leaves that basis open unless you deliberately want an overall judgment.

Choose the method after you have described the options. Comparing labels is not the same as comparing proposals. Make the evidence available and give people a way to identify a knowledge gap.

## How do you run a pairwise comparison?

Run a pairwise comparison by holding the question steady while changing the pair of options. The sequence below is our suggested manual exercise. It demonstrates the judgments, not ChoiceBoard’s ranking algorithm.

1. **Define the question.** State the decision and the factor being considered.
 
2. **Describe the options.** Give participants the same information about each alternative.
 
3. **Present a pair.** Ask for a preference and a reason. Record an unknown or tie explicitly if your chosen method supports it.
 
4. **Record the remaining pairs.** For a complete manual exercise, compare each distinct pair once under the same question.
 
5. **Inspect the pattern.** Look for ties, cycles, and differences between participants before drawing an overall conclusion.

Illustrative complete exercise: three hypothetical options, one participant, one question

| Pair | Recorded preference | Reason to capture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Option A vs. Option B | Option A | The participant’s evidence and reasoning. |
| Option A vs. Option C | Option A | The participant’s evidence and reasoning. |
| Option B vs. Option C | Option B | The participant’s evidence and reasoning. |

These hypothetical preferences are consistent with A above B above C. This example contains no real participant data and does not establish that A is objectively best. It shows one recorded ordering for one question.

## How many pairwise comparisons do you need?

A complete set of distinct pairs contains n(n−1)/2 comparisons, where n is the number of options. The [1000minds guide](https://www.1000minds.com/decision-making/pairwise-comparison) gives the same formula. Five options therefore produce 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 pairs.

Calculated pair counts for one complete set

| Options | Calculation | Distinct pairs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 3 × 2 ÷ 2 | 3 |
| 5 | 5 × 4 ÷ 2 | 10 |
| 10 | 10 × 9 ÷ 2 | 45 |

The count treats A vs. B and B vs. A as the same pair. It excludes comparing an option with itself. It is a count for one complete set, not a promised question count for ChoiceBoard.

If every participant completes every pair for every factor, multiply the pair count by the number of participants and factors. That statement applies only to that exhaustive design. A different sampling or ranking method can use a different set of questions.

## Can pairwise preferences contradict one another?

Pairwise preferences can form a cycle: A is preferred to B, B to C, and C to A. The [method guide’s transitivity discussion](https://www.1000minds.com/decision-making/pairwise-comparison) explains why a set of pair judgments need not provide a consistent ordering.

In the illustrative exercise above, change the A vs. C answer to C. You now have that cycle. Each option has one preferred result and one nonpreferred result, so simple win counts would tie.

Our recommendation is to revisit the reasoning before forcing an order. Check whether the question changed in the participant’s mind, whether information was missing, or whether a trade-off remains unresolved. A cycle is something to investigate, not evidence that a participant’s view should be discarded.

## How is pairwise comparison different from weighted scoring?

Pairwise comparison records judgments between options. A weighted decision matrix combines numeric ratings with criterion weights. The [decision matrix template](https://choiceboard.io/blog/templates/decision-matrix-template/) shows that calculation explicitly.

Decide what you need to inspect after the exercise. If you use ratings, preserve the rating anchors and evidence. If you use pairs, preserve the question and comparison context. Neither format excuses an undefined criterion or an unsupported claim.

## What does ChoiceBoard add to the comparison?

ChoiceBoard collects head-to-head input about options and factors and returns a ranked result with a measured level of agreement. The ranking describes the resulting order; the agreement measure addresses alignment. The person who has to make the call still interprets the result.

> ChoiceBoard doesn’t hide disagreement, it measures it.
> 
> 
> 
> The ChoiceBoard team

Put the comparisons inside a clear [group decision-making process](https://choiceboard.io/blog/guides/group-decision-making-process/). Define who owns the outcome, how participants contribute, and what the final record needs to explain.

## Frequently asked questions

How many pairs are there for five options?

There are 10 distinct pairs: 5 × 4 ÷ 2. This assumes every pair is compared once for one question. It is not a promised question count for a particular product.

Does pairwise comparison always produce a clear winner?

No. Preferences can tie or form a cycle, and different participants can disagree. The result depends on the judgments collected and the method used to combine them.

What is a preference cycle?

A preference cycle occurs when the judgments loop back on themselves, such as A preferred to B, B to C, and C to A. Those judgments do not form one consistent ordering.

Is this manual example ChoiceBoard’s ranking algorithm?

No. The example illustrates pairwise judgments and a simple consistency check. ChoiceBoard’s supplied product description promises a ranked result with a measured level of agreement; this guide does not specify its ranking algorithm.

# Decision matrix template for team choices

You have a shortlist, but each person is judging it against a different standard. This decision matrix template puts the options, criteria, weights, and evidence in one place. Use the blank workbook for your own choice, then inspect the worked example to see how the calculation behaves.

**The ChoiceBoard team** · 5-minute read

Published September 7, 2026 · Updated September 7, 2026

**Key takeaways**

- Weighted scoring multiplies each rating by its criterion’s weight, then adds the results.

- Higher ratings should consistently mean more desirable outcomes.

- A decision matrix’s ratings depend on its underlying assumptions.

- The worked example uses hypothetical weights and ratings, not customer data.

## How do you use this decision matrix template?

Use the decision matrix template by defining three criteria, assigning weights that total 100%, and rating each option on the same scale. The downloadable workbook includes a blank working sheet and a separate illustrative example. Its weighted scores update when you change the inputs.

[Download the decision matrix workbook](https://choiceboard.io/blog/templates/decision-matrix-template/decision-matrix.xlsx)

A weighted decision matrix combines ratings for options with the importance assigned to each criterion. The [American Society for Quality (ASQ)](https://asq.org/quality-resources/decision-matrix) describes multiplying ratings by weights and adding the results for each option.

1. **Define the criteria.** Replace the three criterion labels with factors relevant to your decision. Record what a low and high rating mean.
 
2. **Set the weights.** Enter percentages totaling 100%. These express your priorities, not a universal recommendation.
 
3. **Rate each option.** Use whole-number ratings from one to five in this workbook, with five always meaning more desirable. Leave unknown ratings blank.
 
4. **Review the result.** Check the evidence and unresolved concerns before the decision owner chooses. Write down why the final choice was made.

The blank sheet has space for five options. A row needs an option name, three valid ratings, and complete criterion weights before its total appears. Keep unused option rows blank. The workbook flags incomplete or invalid inputs rather than presenting them as a zero score.

## What does a blank decision matrix look like?

A blank decision matrix needs named options, criteria, and scoring rules before its totals mean anything. Copy this structure into a document if you prefer a manual version. Use the workbook for formulas.

Blank matrix structure: replace bracketed fields

| Option | [Criterion 1] | [Criterion 2] | [Criterion 3] | Weighted total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weight | [Weight %] | [Weight %] | [Weight %] | Weights total 100% |
| [Option name] | [Rating] | [Rating] | [Rating] | Sum of rating × weight |

Keep the reason for each rating alongside the matrix. Our suggested evidence note is: “Source, observation, uncertainty, and reviewer.” A score without its reasoning is difficult to challenge constructively.

## How do you weight criteria in a decision matrix?

Weight criteria by stating how much each factor should influence this particular decision. Agree on the definitions before entering percentages. In this template, the weights total 100% so the weighted result remains on the same one-to-five scale as the ratings.

Keep the direction of the rating scale consistent. ASQ specifically cautions that criteria such as cost can reverse the intended meaning: high cost may deserve a low rating. Name the criterion “Low total cost,” or write explicit anchors for low and high ratings.

Separate requirements from preferences. We recommend checking nonnegotiable requirements before scoring, so a strong rating elsewhere cannot quietly compensate for an unacceptable option. Record the requirement and supporting evidence in the decision notes.

## How is the weighted total calculated?

The weighted total is the sum of each rating multiplied by its weight. The example below assumes three hypothetical options, three criteria, and the stated ratings. It is an arithmetic demonstration, not a vendor evaluation or recommended set of priorities.

Illustrative example: hypothetical weights and ratings

| Option | Low total cost 50% | Implementation fit 30% | Support fit 20% | Weighted total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Option A | 4 | 3 | 2 | 3.3 |
| Option B | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3.5 |
| Option C | 2 | 5 | 3 | 3.1 |

For Option A: (4 × 0.50) + (3 × 0.30) + (2 × 0.20) = 3.3. Option B has the highest total under these assumptions. That is the extent of the result.

Try changing the weights to 20% for low total cost, 60% for implementation fit, and 20% for support fit. The same ratings give A = 3.0, B = 3.8, and C = 4.0. Option C now leads. The change illustrates why the team should discuss the weights, not just the final order.

## What should you do when people disagree with the ranking?

When people disagree with the ranking, inspect the ratings, evidence, and weights separately. Ask which input they would change and why. ASQ notes that ratings are only as sound as the assumptions behind them; the highest total does not necessarily dictate the choice.

Our recommendation is to preserve the disagreement in the evidence notes. If the decision owner chooses a lower-scoring option, record the reason. Do not quietly alter the inputs to make the preferred option win.

## How can you run the decision in ChoiceBoard?

Use the same options and factors to frame a decision in ChoiceBoard. Participants answer head-to-head comparisons, and the result includes a ranking and a measured level of agreement. This is a different input method from entering spreadsheet ratings; it does not imply a workbook import feature.

> ChoiceBoard doesn’t hide disagreement, it measures it.
> 
> 
> 
> The ChoiceBoard team

ChoiceBoard structures the decision. The person who has to make the call still evaluates the result. For the surrounding workflow, read the [group decision-making process](https://choiceboard.io/blog/guides/group-decision-making-process/). For the comparison method, read the [pairwise comparison guide](https://choiceboard.io/blog/guides/pairwise-comparison-method/).

## Frequently asked questions

Do decision matrix weights have to total 100%?

This workbook requires weights totaling 100%. That keeps its weighted totals on the rating scale. Other weighted-scoring implementations can use different weight conventions.

Should a high cost get a high score?

Not when higher scores mean more desirable results. Define the rating direction before scoring. For example, a low total cost can receive a higher desirability rating.

What happens if a rating is missing?

The workbook leaves the weighted total blank and flags the missing input. Enter a rating only when you have a basis for it; do not use zero to represent an unknown.

Does the highest score determine the final decision?

The total summarizes the ratings and weights you entered. Review the assumptions, constraints, and disagreement before choosing. Record the decision owner’s reasoning.
